---
title: "Rank Based Sort"
format: html
---

An excerpt from Frederico Mazzone et al. (CITATION) discusses a solution that applies matrix computation to reduce the comparison depth many sorting methods struggle with. Comparison, swap-based techniques, and arg-max functions that normal sorting methods use are computationally expensive in FHE. We would prefer to use these methods minimally.

With CKKS’s addition, multiplication, and rotation, we can evaluate a sorting method without swapping to elements.

### Methods

To understand the process of the rank-based sorting, we will need the following methods. The methods will be followed with either L or R to signify left and right:

-   CMP (Comparison)

-   IND (Indicator)

-   SUM

-   REPL (Replicate)

-   RANK

-   EQ (Equality)

### Assumption

Before conducting the sort, we need to take care of one main assumption.

-   All elements in the vector are distinct, unless we consider tie corrections

### Rank

First, we need to find the overall order statistics of each element. To find which element is in the “k-th” place, we need to start with the rank function. The rank will allow us to determine which element should be in the i’th position for our sort.

To determine the rank of a vector:

1.  Perform $REPL(v) = A$ to replicate the row vector of n elements into a matrix of n x n.

2.  $CMP(A, A^T)$ to compare the replicated matrix with its transpose

    -   To do so, we will take the difference between the two matrices to output a matrix of -1, 0, 1 values: $A - A^T = M$

3.  Let $M = sign(M)$ isolating the positive values to create a matrix of just 0 and 1

4.  $R = SUM(M)$ by summing either the columns or rows depending on the initial difference matrix, we will have a final output of the statistic rank from 0 to n-1

5.  $R = R + 1$ by adding 1 to each element in R, we will end with a vector of ranks 1 to n

### Rank-Based Sort

To sort a vector of degree n, we need the following:

-   A matrix of replicated rows of our input

-   A matrix of replicated rank row vectors (Matrix A)

-   A plain text constant matrix with all elements in each row being one singular number from 1 to n (Matrix B)

The process goes as follows:

1.  $C = IND( A - B )$ to set all elements that are 0 to value 1 with rest being 0
2.  Take the product of our replicated matrix and the indicator matrix $P = C * A$
3.  Sum the columns $f = SUM(P)$
4.  By transposing our final matrix, we will then end with a sorted row vector $f$

### Ties

When a given vector includes non distinct elements, we will have to perform a tie correction.

To do so, we will need the following:

-   A matrix of replicated rows of our input: A

-   An upper triangular matrix U

To do so:

1.  We will first create an equality matrix by comparing the replicated matrix and it's transpose outputting 1 if the index is equal and 0 else.

    $M1 = EQ( A, A^T)$

2.  Multiply M1 with a upper triangular matrix to convert the tie elements into two distinct elements

    $M2 = M1 * U$

3.  $s1 = SUM(M1)$ and $s2 = SUM(M2)$

4.  $O=s1-s2$

    -   This final vector will have offset values of only 1 and 0.

5.  $t = R + O$ where $t$ will be our final rank vector by conducting the sum of the original ranks and the offset

The example below works through $x = [30, 10, 10, 20]$, with the entries belonging to the tied values in orange.

```{=latex}
\newcommand{\tied}[1]{\textcolor[RGB]{230,159,0}{\mathbf{#1}}}
```

:::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: hidden
$$
\newcommand{\tied}[1]{\textcolor[RGB]{230,159,0}{\mathbf{#1}}}
$$
:::
::::

$$
\overset{A}{\begin{bmatrix}
30 & \tied{10} & \tied{10} & 20 \\
30 & \tied{10} & \tied{10} & 20 \\
30 & \tied{10} & \tied{10} & 20 \\
30 & \tied{10} & \tied{10} & 20
\end{bmatrix}}
==
\overset{A^T}{\begin{bmatrix}
30 & 30 & 30 & 30 \\
\tied{10} & \tied{10} & \tied{10} & \tied{10} \\
\tied{10} & \tied{10} & \tied{10} & \tied{10} \\
20 & 20 & 20 & 20
\end{bmatrix}}
=
\overset{M_1}{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \tied{1} & \tied{1} & 0 \\
0 & \tied{1} & \tied{1} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}}
$$

**Step 1.** Replicate $x$ into the rows of $A$, so $A_{ij} = x_j$ and $A^T_{ij} = x_i$. Then compare the two entry by entry: $(M_1)_{ij} = 1$ if $A_{ij} = A^T_{ij}$, and 0 otherwise.

$$
\overset{M_1}{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \tied{1} & \tied{1} & 0 \\
0 & \tied{1} & \tied{1} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}}
\odot
\overset{U}{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
0 & \tied{1} & \tied{1} & 1 \\
0 & \tied{0} & \tied{1} & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}}
=
\overset{M_2}{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \tied{1} & \tied{1} & 0 \\
0 & \tied{0} & \tied{1} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}}
$$

**Step 2.** Multiply $M_1$ entry by entry with an upper triangular matrix of ones, where $U_{ij} = 1$ if $i \le j$ and 0 otherwise. This gives $(M_2)_{ij} = (M_1)_{ij} \, U_{ij}$, which drops the matches below the diagonal.

$$
\overset{s_1}{\begin{bmatrix}
1 \\
\tied{2} \\
\tied{2} \\
1
\end{bmatrix}}
-
\overset{s_2}{\begin{bmatrix}
1 \\
\tied{2} \\
\tied{1} \\
1
\end{bmatrix}}
=
\overset{O}{\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
\tied{0} \\
\tied{1} \\
0
\end{bmatrix}}
\qquad\qquad
\overset{R}{\begin{bmatrix}
4 \\
\tied{1} \\
\tied{1} \\
3
\end{bmatrix}}
+
\overset{O}{\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
\tied{0} \\
\tied{1} \\
0
\end{bmatrix}}
=
\overset{t}{\begin{bmatrix}
4 \\
\tied{1} \\
\tied{2} \\
3
\end{bmatrix}}
$$

**Step 3.** Sum the rows of each matrix, so $(s_1)_i = \sum_j (M_1)_{ij}$ and $(s_2)_i = \sum_j (M_2)_{ij}$. Subtract them to get the offset $O$, then add $O$ to the ranks $R$ so tied values get different ranks in $t$.
